units.text: The expression ‘law of nature’ shelters claims that do not all work the same way. If we judge them by a single template, we will declare some disciplines insufficiently scientific and grant others a precision they do not possess.

A dynamical law describes how a state evolves. We know the state at a given time, specify interactions and try to calculate what follows. In a deterministic model, complete initial data and the same rule yield the same evolution. The word ‘complete’ does much work. In practice, data are finite and the problem may be highly sensitive to errors.

A probabilistic law describes distributions of outcomes, not necessarily the individual outcome. If a model assigns an event a probability of one quarter, its occurrence does not refute the model, nor does its nonoccurrence in a single trial. Evaluation requires series, comparable conditions and procedures accounting for random variation. Claiming that every individual surprise violates a probabilistic law means demanding something other than what the model asserts.

A conservation principle says a quantity is preserved under relevant conditions. It is not necessarily a complete instruction for every movement. Knowing the total money in a system of accounts does not alone tell us who makes the next transfer. Conservation restricts possibilities without always choosing a single one. The accounting analogy explains a constraint’s role; it does not turn energy into currency.

Constitutive laws describe the response of a particular material type: the relationship between stress and strain, or current and voltage under a particular regime. Some are excellent approximations. Their domain is not a hidden defect but part of their meaning. A material model can have parameters dependent on temperature and history without making every prediction impossible.

Then there are scaling regularities in which one quantity varies as a power of another. Such a fit may suggest a mechanism but does not identify it alone. Multiple processes can produce similar mathematical forms. A straight line in a convenient representation begins an investigation; it does not prove that the same principle governs cities, organisms and markets.

Another type of principle formulates limits or impossibilities: which operations cannot be performed within a theory with particular resources and conditions. Such a prohibition can be stronger than a specific prediction. But the premises must be retained. ‘It cannot be built in this model’ does not automatically mean ‘it cannot exist in any logically conceivable reality’.

These differences are supplemented by a separate axis: fundamental or effective. An effective law describes a domain of energies, scales or conditions without claiming to enumerate all ultimate mechanisms. Effective theories are not mere patches awaiting truth. They can systematically organize which effects matter and how large neglected corrections are (Burgess, 2007) .

In research practice, ‘fundamental’ does not mean we possess the universe’s final certificate. It may mean fundamental relative to the current framework or a level of explanation. We should be alert when a methodological adjective turns, without argument, into a metaphysical verdict.

Physical laws must also be distinguished from mathematical truths. A theorem shows what follows from axioms and definitions. To use it about the world, we must still justify the correspondence between the formal structure and the investigated system. We can prove a result perfectly about a model that describes its object poorly. Deductive rigor does not automatically repair the choice of premises.

No definition is an empirical discovery merely because it carries symbols. If we define a quantity as the ratio of two others, the relationship is true by convention; what needs investigation is how those quantities behave and why the definition helps. Sometimes confusion arises precisely when an accounting identity or definition is presented as a causal explanation.

This atlas offers a simple discipline. Before asking whether a law is true, we ask what kind of claim it is, what domain it has, what data would count against it and which part of the conclusion comes from definitions. The word ‘law’ does not replace these questions. A science book becomes more useful by explaining differences than by collecting formulas under the same solemn label.
